The GDPx leaderboard now looks like this: It’s worth emphasizing that certain models like Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra have sandbagged overall scores due to their safety classifiers. posts.title: Distilling Kimi-K3.1-Pro into Qwen3.8-27B: Teaching a model a new language
posts.summary: Qwen3.8-27B answered in Thai when asked for Lao. We distilled Kimi-K3.1-Pro's Lao translation into it with Together Post-Training: 93% of the teacher's score, with Thai intact. Code and costs included.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Finding the gap | The plan: off-policy distillation | The Thai surprise | Fixing Thai | Closing the rest of the Lao gap | Results | Training on five languages | If you have a gap like this While running some experiments we found out that Qwen3.8-27B , one of the most popular small language models (SLMs), can't write Lao, a Southwestern Tai language and the official language of Laos. If you ask it to translate an English sentence into Lao, it answers in Thai, Lao's closest relative, which uses an entirely different script. On the FLORES-200 Lao test set, the model scores 5.5 chrF++, a 0 to 100 score for how closely a translation matches a human reference, and only 11% of its outputs are in Lao script. Kimi-K3.1-Pro scores 47.5 on the same test. Admittedly, this is a niche use case, but the pattern is quite common: a small language model displays jagged intelligence, falling flat on a narrow task you care about while a larger, more expensive model handles it with ease. To fix this, we used Kimi-K3.1-Pro as a teacher and distilled its Lao translation ability into Qwen3.8-27B using Together Post-Training. After training on about 3,800 of Kimi-K3.1-Pro's translations, the 27B student answers in Lao on every test sentence and scores 44.3, which is 93% of the teacher's score. It also kept its Thai translation ability, which interestingly turned out to be the hardest part. Our first attempt fixed Lao within 25 training steps but also lost Thai translating capabilities along with it. This post walks through how we found the gap and what ended up working. The code…

posts.title: Sequence-level RL for diffusion language models
posts.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are emerging as a promising alternative to traditional autoregressive LLMs. Unlike autoregressive models, which generate text one token at a time, diffusion models iteratively refine sequences through a denoising process, offering the potential for parallel generation and more flexible decoding.

However, most existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods are designed for autoregressive models, making them challenging to adapt effectively to the distinct generation process of diffusion LLMs. In the collaborative paper Principled RL for Diffusion LLMs Emerges from a Sequence-Level Perspective , accepted to ICLR 2026, researchers from Lambda, Stanford University, Renmin University of China, and Tsinghua University introduce ELBO-based Sequence-level Policy Optimization (ESPO), a principled RL framework designed specifically for diffusion language models. ESPO delivers substantial improvements across planning, mathematical reasoning, and coding benchmarks while promoting stable and effective training. Traditional RL methods for language models, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), typically rely on token-level probability estimates. While well suited to autoregressive generation, these approaches do not naturally align with diffusion models, which iteratively predict and refine tokens across an entire sequence. Inference workloads often need to connect securely to external data or services, like loading private weights from cloud storage or fetching LoRA adapters at request time. The easiest way to set that up is with a permanent cloud key and open internet access, but that gives the model far more access than it needs—and it's easy to exploit. Each deployment should access only the resources it needs, without risking exposure of credentials or data. Baseten gives you controls to set boundaries on that access. OpenID Connect (OIDC) replaces permanent cloud keys with short-lived tokens tied to a specific deployment, so each credential works only for the job it was issued for and expires automatically. The Baseten Delivery Network (BDN) mirrors your weights once into a read-only volume, so serving replicas never need access to your bucket. Egress restrictions also limit outbound connections to the hosts a model actually calls, so a compromised container can't reach anywhere else. posts.title: RDMA memory registration overhead in GPU VMs explained
posts.summary: RDMA memory registration uses host memory your VM never sees. Learn where it goes, how Crusoe caps it per VF, and when to trade guest RAM for headroom.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Where the hidden memory goes | Why RDMA memory registration overhead grows with GPU scale | Which workloads drive the cost | How Crusoe keeps every tenant safe | Measuring the hidden memory allocation | Size the budget from fleet data | Enforcing limits on NIC firmware | Apply it on every host Every GPU buffer registered for RDMA costs host memory outside your VM, and at GPU scale that can reach gigabytes per NIC. Crusoe bounds the cost with a per-VF budget in NIC firmware, and a few changes keep most workloads well within it. Your workload registers GPU memory (HBM) for remote direct memory access (RDMA) inside a VM. Each call succeeds and returns a key, and inside the guest nothing else changes. On the host, the network card takes memory to keep track of what you registered, and no process shows it. RDMA lets a network card read and write a buffer directly, without involving the remote CPU or operating system, so the card keeps a record of every buffer it may touch and every connection it serves. Its on-chip memory is far too small to hold that record, so the record lives in host RAM that your VM cannot see. Most workloads in our fleet keep this RDMA memory registration overhead under about 1 GiB per NIC, but RDMA-heavy ones, like disaggregated inference and mixture-of-experts (MoE) training, have pushed a single NIC to between 4 and 6 GiB. This post follows that memory from the registration call down to the host and shows why the cost grows with the amount of GPU memory you register. It then explains how Crusoe keeps one VM's registrations from affecting…

Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work. But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite , and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything . Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it. We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. posts.excerpt: Sections: TL;DR | Why is it hard to run a PyTorch model with TensorRT on a robot? | How it works | Getting started | Install | Export, in Python | Run, in Python, without torch | Run, in C++ We talked about this work at PyTorch Conference 2026: Deploying Robot Policies Across Many Targets with ExecuTorch . GR00T 1.7 (3B) on a Jetson Orin Nano 8GB: about 200 ms per action chunk. A robot runs its models on its own computer, like NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor or a custom board, and they have to finish on time. A policy, the model that decides what the robot does next, returns a short plan at a time, called an action chunk, say 50 actions. If the next chunk isn’t ready when the robot finishes the current one, the robot stops and waits. And everything shares the same memory: the CPU, the GPU, the cameras and every model. Offloading to a server adds a network round trip, which can easily take 100 ms, over a link the robot can’t always count on. On NVIDIA hardware the fastest way to run a model is TensorRT , NVIDIA’s inference compiler. Until now, getting a PyTorch model into TensorRT meant one of four things: Today we’re adding a new way: Torch-TensorRT 2.15 compiles the model with TensorRT and saves it as an ExecuTorch 1.6 program that runs without libtorch. It skips ONNX and captures the model with PyTorch’s own torch.export . If TensorRT can’t convert part of the model, preprocessing included, you can send that part to ExecuTorch’s CUDA backend, which runs it on the GPU in the same program on the same CUDA stream instead of failing the build. Many teams store fine-tuned and proprietary model weights in private Hugging Face repos. Deploying those models on an external platform has usually meant handing over a long-lived access token that works until someone deletes it. Hugging Face Trusted Publishers improved on this by issuing short-lived tokens at deploy time, but until recently, those tokens could also write to your repo, which is more access than a deployment needs. To maintain a high bar for security, we wanted to go further: no long-lived credentials anywhere, and no access beyond pulling the weights. We asked Hugging Face for a read-only option, and they shipped it within days. Trusted Publishers now supports read-only access, so inference providers get a 1-hour token that can only pull from a single repo and can't modify it. We're proud to be the first inference provider to support read-only Trusted Publishers, joining our existing OIDC support for pulling weights from S3 and GCS. We'll keep working with partners across the industry to make workload identity and scoped access controls the default for AI infrastructure. posts.title: Enabling Mid-Epoch Training Resumption with Ray Train
posts.summary: Mid-epoch resumption in Ray Train saves the data loader's state with each checkpoint, so a restarted job resumes mid-epoch instead of starting over.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: The cost of mid-epoch training failures | How it works | Saving progress | Restoring progress | Using mid-epoch resumption | Requirements | Evaluating the impact | Summary Training failures are increasingly common at scale, and effective training infrastructure is judged by how quickly it recovers from them. Mid-epoch resumption lets Ray Train and Ray Data checkpoint your data loader alongside your model, so your restarted run picks up where its last checkpoint left off without breaking exactly-once training. Here's what it gives you: Less repeated work: a restarted job picks up from its last checkpoint, instead of starting the epoch over. Correct data coverage: every row is still trained on exactly once per epoch, even across failures. Simple adoption: it works with your existing Ray Train checkpoints and requires minimal changes to your training script. In our benchmark, with mid-epoch resumption, a training job that failed 75% of the way through an epoch achieved 9% faster overall runtime and 9% lower dollar cost than when it skipped batches to resume. The bigger your epochs, the more it saves you on failure. Mid-epoch resumption will ship with Ray 2.61 and is currently available in the Anyscale Runtime starting with Ray version 2.50. Mid-epoch training failures can be costly. Picture a run whose latest checkpoint was saved 75% of the way through an epoch, followed by a worker failure at 80%: The model restores from the 75% checkpoint, but the data loader has no record of where it was. posts.title: Announcing vLLM-GR: Efficient Inference for Generative Recommendation
posts.summary: vLLM-GR extends vLLM to serve generative recommendation models with accelerator-side beam search, catalog constraints, and shared KV caching across candidate paths.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: About | Why vLLM-GR? | Inside the Architecture | Key Features | Performance Evaluation | Future Roadmap | Getting Started | Installation Today we’re introducing vLLM-GR , an open-source inference and serving framework built on vLLM for generative recommendation models. Consider a video feed. Given a viewer’s history, a model such as OneRec can generate a semantic ID (SID) for a video the viewer might watch next. To assemble a feed, the application needs a set of candidates. vLLM-GR extends vLLM’s model execution and paged key-value (KV) cache with beam search that explores multiple candidate IDs in one request. posts.title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
posts.summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: TL;DR | How a KV pool works on vLLM | At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM | DRAM only buffers writes and stages reads | Longer prompts | Why NVMe keeps up | What NVMe buys: retention | What it costs: DRAM per TB held, NVMe per TB written Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload…

Performance alone tells only part of the story: how much energy does it take to complete a simulation, predict a protein structure, or generate a protein design? Floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) per watt measures computational efficiency, while power usage effectiveness (PUE) describes facility overhead. Both are useful, but neither directly measures application output. Science per joule makes that connection: atom-timesteps per joule for molecular dynamics, simulated days per joule for climate models, or predictions and designs per joule for AI biology workloads. The idea builds on established energy-to-solution metrics, including those described for the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) . Dense attention scores every query against every key, so its cost per query grows with the context length N, and at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer. Part 2: KubeRay in production: best practices from the field covers how teams run KubeRay in production and how Anyscale KubeRay Connect fits on top of it. The Anyscale platform has built-in observability for Ray workloads, and KubeRay Connect , introduced at the end of Part 2, brings it to the KubeRay clusters you already run. This post covers one of those features, built specifically for training workloads: Ray Train's data ingest observability. Model training is capital-intensive, so training teams need to pay close attention to GPU utilization. At the scale of hundreds or thousands of GPUs, even a small slowdown adds up to a lot of lost GPU-hours. To keep GPUs busy, the next batch of data needs to be ready the moment the model finishes the current one. When it isn't, the GPUs sit and wait. That's GPU starvation, and it's one of the most common reasons utilization drops. It's also one of the quietest: nothing crashes, nothing alerts, and the job just keeps running a little slower than it should. Teams usually notice one of two symptoms: GPU utilization that swings up and down instead of holding steady, or training runs that take longer than expected. posts.title: Last year we built megakernels. This year we deleted them: The road to Together Compiler
posts.summary: Together Compiler uses AI agents to rewrite and fuse the GPU kernels in a model’s forward pass. It beats hand-written megakernels by 28% on B200 (2,118 vs 1,649 tokens/s on Llama 3.2 1B). This is how we got from one to the other.

posts.excerpt: Sections: Introduction | Part 1: Torch Compile | How Torch Compile Works | Finding #1: Compiler heuristics cannot reliably select the best implementation across workloads. | Finding #2: The fastest kernel in isolation isn't necessarily the fastest during inference. | Finding #3: Inductor leaves fusion opportunities on the table. | What these findings pointed to | Part 2: Megakernels AI inference is becoming increasingly heterogeneous. New model architectures are released every week, inference traffic shifts across different batch sizes and sequence lengths, and hardware platforms continue to proliferate. Achieving peak performance across all these regimes demands optimization frameworks that can keep up. Last year, we helped release some of the first AI megakernels , where we executed an entire model forward pass within a single, highly fused GPU kernel. They reached record breaking speeds, but it was difficult to put them in production. After months of effort, we had a grand total of one model, one batch size, and one customer. This year, we examined what we could simplify and discovered something surprising. With just CUDA Graphs and PDL on top of default Torch Inductor kernels, we could recover 98% of megakernel performance without writing a single kernel. And with “multi-kernels” and agent loops, we could further beat our old megakernels by up to 1.7x, achieving over 1100 TPS for Llama 1B on H100. posts.title: Making open models work for long-horizon agentic workloads
posts.summary: Every agent turn resends the full session. Together AI and Ollama break down how to protect the prefix cache, from the harness to the GPU.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: What an agent turn looks like to a GPU | Cache is king | The harnesses and APIs | Loading tools late | Things at the top that change | Reasoning effort | Big tool results | Subagents Coding agents send the whole conversation again on every turn. Prefix caching keeps the inference engine from redoing that work, but only if the harness leaves the start of the prompt alone and the engine sends each turn back to the GPU that already has it cached. Together AI and Ollama work on opposite sides of that handoff, so we wrote down what each, the client side and the inference engine side, needs to do to successfully build agentic apps. Coding agents have an odd traffic pattern. Every time the agent takes a step, the harness sends the model the entire conversation so far: the system prompt, every tool definition, your request, every file the agent has read, and every command it has run. What comes back is usually a tool call a few dozen tokens long. Then it happens again, with everything from last time plus a little more. This large input sequence length (ISL) and small output sequence length (OSL) is characteristic of most agentic workloads. If the GPU had to work through that whole transcript from scratch on every turn, long sessions would get slower and more expensive with every step. Prefix caching is what saves most of that work. The problem is that if you’re not careful it's also very easy to break the prefix cache. We come at this problem from opposite ends. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory. As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows. GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). posts.title: Modular at LLVM Developers' Meeting 2026
posts.summary: As GPUs get faster, the cost of CPU-to-accelerator communication grows until it takes up much of the inference time. Device graphs address that by submitting a whole sequence of work to the device at once. MAX uses them, and so does every widely used serving stack. The usual way to build one is record and replay: capture a stream of commands at runtime, then replay it. CUDA and HIP both offer this.

posts.excerpt: Sections: Choosing a target for quantization | Low-precision formats on Blackwell | Block-scaled backward passes | Re-quantization with stochastic rounding | Quantized communications | Kernels for low-precision training | Recipe details | Closing thoughts Training large language models involves calculating and storing a lot of numbers. Using fewer bits for each value reduces memory usage and allows GPUs to perform calculations faster. However, there is a tradeoff: fewer bits also mean fewer representable numbers, leading to more aggressive rounding. Lower-precision representations ultimately hurt accuracy by adding error to the calculations. For example, suppose we want to store the number 3.2, but the nearest values our numerical format can represent are 3 and 4. Rounding to 3 introduces a quantization error of − 0.2 , the difference between the actual value and the one that can be represented in the quantized format. A single error like this may seem small, but these errors accumulate over training as rounding happens repeatedly across layers and optimization steps, which can impair the learning process. This is the central challenge of low-precision training: how can we benefit from faster arithmetic without introducing errors that interfere with learning? We manage this tradeoff through our use of three key numerical formats during training: BF16, MXFP8, and NVFP4. Each format’s precision is fixed, but its speed depends on the hardware being used. Take a coding agent: the Sandbox sits nearly idle while the model reasons about what to do next, and spikes only when the agent installs dependencies, runs tests, or builds the project. The same pattern shows up in other common Sandbox workloads: RL rollouts, evals, and app builders. Today, most sandboxes are priced based on a fixed-resource reservation model. Reservations are a poor fit for spiky work, for two reasons: We believe your bill should align with your workload, rising when it’s busy and falling when it’s idle. That’s why our Sandboxes burst: a Sandbox gets the CPU and memory it needs when your work spikes and gives them back when it is done. You pay for what you actually use. Every Sandbox bursts by default. Start with the base 0.125 cores and 128 MiB request and let your Sandbox grow as it needs. With active-resource pricing, you pay each second for what you use, with the small request as a floor. You can request more to guarantee it, but you’ll pay for those resources even when your Sandbox is idle. Helion, PyTorch’s domain-specific language (DSL) for performance portable machine learning kernels, relies heavily on autotuning for its performance. Autotuning time can be a major bottleneck: for example, a previous team tuning a single paged-attention kernel across 72 shapes spent 10 hours in Helion’s quick mode, and 25 at full effort. To address these issues, we’ve developed a set of heuristics that read a kernel’s IR and dataflow at compile time and emit a config directly, without any autotuning . We classify kernels into broad families based on the operations they contain – matmul, reduction, or pointwise – and apply a family-specific heuristic to each. These families are intentionally general: the matmul heuristic, for example, looks for any kernel containing a matmul operation such as hl.dot or torch.baddbmm, not just standard m-n-k matrix multiplications. These are designed to be generic and apply broadly to custom kernels that users may write. A single Helion kernel can lower into thousands of different Triton kernels. Choosing an inference provider matters as much as choosing the model itself. When you use a closed model through its direct API, model capability and inference come as one package. With open-weight models, you can choose among providers that serve the same model or deploy it on your own infrastructure. Providers use different software, hardware, and operating practices to serve the same model. These differences affect answer quality, wait times, and the cost of completing a task. They also shape how the service handles failures and processes your data. This article explains the engineering behind these differences and uses the five dimensions in Figure 1 to guide your evaluation of an inference partner. The same model can deliver different answer quality and tool-use reliability across providers. Differences come from how each provider configures the model, executes computations, and parses output. Models like GR2 (Generative Reasoning Re-ranker) [ arXiv:2606.31984 ] have demonstrated that generative reasoning can meaningfully improve re-ranking quality. The next question is: for large-scale ranking and decision systems, how small can the policy model be without losing that generative reasoning capability? A 0.6B dense student distilled from stronger teachers could serve with much lower latency and cost, enabling broader traffic coverage, faster model refreshes, and more RL experiments per day. That requires the whole training cycle to be fast, and model FLOPs are only one part of it. At 0.6B parameters, rollout generation, synchronization, and framework overhead take a growing share of wall-clock time. Because a 0.6B model has far less matrix arithmetic per layer than frontier dense or MoE models, fixed system overheads (host dispatch, synchronization, and KV-cache lifecycle) shift the bottleneck from FLOPs to coordination. Most of the engineering in v0.1.0 went into three places where that matters: how steps are launched, how much of a step lives in one kernel, and where the KV cache sits when it is not on the device. This blog covers what ships in v0.1.0 and where it goes next. We start with how the backend is built: the plugin architecture, the asynchronous runtime, megakernels, prefill-decode disaggregation over EFA, HiCache, and SGLang Diffusion on Neuron. It takes a significant amount of time between moves. This document presents a design and tested implementation for getting that under a second by moving the search into a Ray cluster. A robot perceives a partial observation of the environment, selects an action via some policy, executes it through a controller, and repeats this at control-loop frequency. Classically, each of those three functions is solved in closed form, and a CPU on the robot is enough to run all of them. Classical robotics built each of those three boxes from first principles: hand-derived kinematics for perception, trajectory optimization for planning, PID or model-predictive controllers for control. This approach, depicted in Figure 1, underlies decades of industrial automation, but every new task, object, or environment typically requires new engineering. Physical AI aims to replace some or all of those boxes with networks trained on data, trading hand-derived precision for generality: a model trained on sufficient data transfers to situations not explicitly programmed for. posts.summary: Cloudflare is building an experimental consensus service using a never-before-deployed consensus algorithm, QuePaxa. In this post we explain how QuePaxa works and why we chose it.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: What we’re building and why it’s unique | The challenges of consensus at a global scale | Destructive interference and leaders | When leader recovery is unstable | When fault detection goes awry | When fault detection is slow | Why QuePaxa is the right fit | How QuePaxa works under the hood Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. Qwen3.5 interleaves full attention with linear-attention layers. Kimi K3 pairs KDA linear attention with MLA, and K3.1 replaces the MLA layers with DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). Their demands do not scale together. A long-context workload grows full-attention KV; many short concurrent requests need more window KV and state slots even though each request’s history is small. The pressure can shift within one request, too: its state slots are taken when it starts, while its full-attention KV keeps growing. SGLang’s default design gives each kind of state its own pool, a sub-pool , and fixes their sizes at startup through --swa-full-tokens-ratio and --mamba-full-memory-ratio . The right ratio depends on traffic you do not know yet. A long-context workload can exhaust the full-attention pool while much of the pool for the bounded states (window KV and recurrent state) sits idle, and many short requests do the reverse. Pulling a 3.6 GB NVIDIA CUDA® image from a registry in the same region took 51.5 seconds. Pulling it from NVIDIA's public registry over the internet took 56.2 seconds. Download and unpack overlap, and unpack is the long pole. In our measurements on 7 GB and 13 GB images, unpack accounted for about 80% of total pull time, and containerd unpacks layers one at a time by default. Many public container images are compressed with gzip, a format from the early 1990s, and decompressing them is what makes unpack slow. The main change is attention: K3.1 Pro adds Sparse Attention (DSA) to all 24 full-attention layers for efficiency. vLLM supports it on day 0 on NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, Google TPUs and Alibaba T-Head Zhenwu PPUs. Each sparse attention layer has a small indexer next to its MLA attention. The indexer keeps one FP8 key per token (132 bytes with its scale) and scores every earlier token for each query with 32 lightweight heads. Then it keeps the top 2,048 tokens. MLA attention then runs exactly, but only over those 2,048 tokens. DSA was introduced in DeepSeek-V3.2; our DeepSeek-V3.2 post covers the indexer in more detail. The payoff is largest in long-context decode, which is bound by memory bandwidth. Dense MLA reads 576 bytes of FP8 latent per context token per layer. DSA still scans the whole context, but only the 132-byte index keys. It then reads the full latent for just 2,048 tokens. At long context, that is about 23% of the bytes dense MLA reads per layer. Your sandbox needs to fetch a document from your backend, submit the result of a task, or call an internal service. Before serving that request, your backend needs to know who is asking and what they should be allowed to do. A shared API key can authenticate the request, but it doesn’t identify which sandbox sent it. You could issue a separate credential for every sandbox, then build the machinery to distribute, rotate, and track those credentials. We built E2B Workload Identity to make this easier. E2B supplies a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) identifying the project, sandbox, and execution behind a request. Your service can verify that identity and apply its own access rules. For us, this is another part of making sandboxes useful for real applications. Your agents need access to your systems, and your systems need a reliable way to identify them. When creating a sandbox, you define a named workload token and its audience, that is, the service you intend to receive it. Then you reference that token in a network rule. When a matching HTTPS request leaves the sandbox, E2B adds a signed token to the request header you configured. E2B handles token issuance outside the sandbox, keeping the token out of the sandbox’s environment and filesystem. The token carries an expiration and the intended audience. Our first annual conference opens today, bringing together leaders from AI-native startups, global enterprises, open-weight model labs, and more. Not even four digits, just the number 4. The other seven keys were similarly weak: 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237. The next day, we wrote a blog post on the immediate action we took to mitigate this leak, and what customers needed to do on their end to stay secure. We extended DeepSeek's Mega MoE kernel with a fast, overlapping backward pass, making it usable for training and delivering a significant speedup: In an MoE model, each token is routed to only a small subset of the model's experts. Those experts live on different GPUs, so training requires a lot of communication between them. In every layer, tokens are sent to the GPU that holds their expert, the expert computation runs, and the results are sent back. This happens twice per layer on every step: once in the forward pass and once in the backward pass. Normally these steps are separate operations. The GPU sorts the tokens, hands them to the transport layer and waits; then it runs the expert math, hands the results back to the transport layer and waits again. All of that waiting wastes GPU time. The question is whether we can overlap compute with communication and close the bubbles in the pipeline. Mega MoE is a fused, overlapping kernel from DeepSeek's open-source DeepGEMM kernel collection. It replaces the chain of separate operations above with a single kernel invocation that handles both computation and communication directly, without round trips from the GPU back to the CPU. It is a compilation problem with many legitimate answers. For example, when NVIDIA TensorRT builds an engine, it makes interdependent decisions about graph-IR transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. This process is called scheduling. Different scheduling choices can preserve model semantics yet produce very different inference performance, making scheduling central to deep learning compiler optimization. No single scheduling strategy is best for every model and deployment environment. A transformation that accelerates one network may slow another. A kernel that is faster in isolation may interact poorly with fusion, tensor layouts, or memory traffic elsewhere in the graph. These coupled, model-dependent effects often appear only after the complete engine is built and measured, making the right strategy increasingly difficult to predict. Low-precision inference usually comes with a tradeoff: faster execution for larger numerical errors. Four-bit weights and activations would appear to be the fastest possible option, while higher precision means sacrificing speed. The benefits of low precision come from both the decreased memory traffic from low precision data and higher hardware throughput for low precision computation. In the decode phase, data traffic dominates while arithmetic capacity sits idle. Therefore, four bit storage is valuable while four bit computation offers no speed advantage. Thus, we keep weights in NVFP4 but let activations stay in BF16. This keeps almost all the memory traffic benefits of having both in NVFP4. For large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the standard options are horizontal scaling, which adds another complete replica, and vertical scaling, which restarts the deployment with a wider expert-parallel topology. Horizontal scaling keeps the current service running, but adds the full model footprint. Vertical scaling can reach the required topology with a smaller increment, but requires rebuilding distributed state, reloading the model, and warming the new deployment. Elastic scale-up is based on principles already implemented in the recovery flow. In recovery, active membership changes unexpectedly; with scale-up, the change is planned and new GPU ranks are added at runtime. Elastic EP Scaling adds four ranks to the running deployment instead of allocating another 20-GPU replica or replacing the job. LLMs generate text auto-regressively, predicting one token at a time. At small batch sizes, decoding relies on "thin" matrix multiplications that underutilize GPU compute because they are limited by memory bandwidth. Batching requests from multiple users turns these operations into larger matrix multiplications and improves overall throughput, but it can reduce the token generation rate experienced by each user. Speculative decoding addresses this need for faster responses by using a lightweight model to draft several tokens, which the target model then verifies together. Verifying multiple tokens increases the amount of computation performed for each read of the model weights, making better use of otherwise idle GPU compute. With the appropriate verification procedure, speculative decoding preserves the target model's output distribution. The EAGLE family is one approach to speculative decoding used in production. Its lightweight transformer drafter takes hidden states and token embeddings from the target model and is trained to predict the target model's output tokens. posts.title: How Modern LLM Architectures Reshape Agent Inference
posts.summary: Hybrid LLMs like Kimi K3 change what inference runtimes must cache. FriendliAI explains prefix reuse, state management, and speculative decoding for agents.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Growing Contexts and Caching Prefixes | Three Architectural Approaches to Long-Context Scaling | Hybrid State and Prefix Reuse in Kimi K3 | Managing State Bundles in the Inference Runtime | From Architectural Efficiency to Serving Performance | General FAQ | What is FriendliAI? | How does FriendliAI reduce inference costs? Agent workloads involve long, growing contexts across multiple model calls. As a task progresses, successive calls share a common prefix, with new messages and tool results appended to the end. Supporting these workloads requires both model architectures and inference runtimes that scale efficiently as context grows. Modern LLM architectures address this scaling challenge by changing how they represent and access history, such as reducing per-token state or compressing history into a fixed-size recurrent state. These approaches change what an inference runtime must retain and reuse. The latest open-weight models combine multiple approaches, making state management a concern that extends beyond the conventional KV cache. In this article, we examine the architectural and runtime changes needed to scale inference for long-context agent workloads. Using Kimi K3 as a case study, we show how hybrid architectures represent a shared prefix as a bundle of attention and recurrent states. We then explore the implications for prefix reuse, cache management, and speculative decoding, focusing on how runtimes must handle these states to realize the model architecture’s efficiency gains. It's built on Google's TorchTPU stack and runs the model definitions that already live in vLLM, so most models that work in vLLM today can be served on TPU without changes to the model code. This work comes out of the engineering partnership between Inferact and Google we announced last month. Our goals for the project are to: vllm-torchtpu is an out-of-tree vLLM platform plugin. Once installed, vLLM picks it up automatically through the vllm.platform_plugins entry point. Models run through vLLM's standard model runner and are compiled with torch.compile(backend="tpu") , which lowers to XLA. Each TPU device gets its own worker process, the same way vLLM runs on GPUs, and communication between devices goes through torch.distributed . This means the scheduler, workers, KV cache manager, and API server are all unmodified upstream vLLM. The TPU-specific work sits underneath them, mostly in a set of JAX/Pallas kernels that are registered as custom ops and called from inside the compiled graph. With its planned Apache 2.0 release, Beam is designed for developers to deploy and build on across the runtimes, frameworks, and coding harnesses they already use. SGLang now supports Beam natively and powers Reflection’s production API. It helps developers translate Beam’s inference efficiency into practical and production-proven serving performance. BF16, NVFP4, and dynamic FP8 support provide flexibility across precision and memory requirements; DFlash2 speculative decoding accelerates generation; and prefix caching with hybrid-attention memory management enables efficient reuse of context across agent interactions. posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Agent workloads are more than just long prompts | KV-cache retention shapes serving performance | Tool use evolves during agent execution | How a trajectory unfolds determines total serving demand | Takeaway: Efficient agent serving requires optimizing the whole trajectory tl;dr: In collaboration with researchers at UIUC and Intel, we evaluated ReAct-style agent workloads across complete trajectories. Serving demand depends on how each trajectory unfolds, whether cached state survives, and how tool use evolves. Serving systems must therefore manage scheduling, cached state, and resources across the complete trajectory rather than optimize individual model calls in isolation. Traditional LLM serving is built around individual requests. A prompt comes in, the model generates a response, and the request completes. Each request is treated independently. The serving stack is designed to batch as many of these independent requests as possible, keep the GPUs busy, and optimize for metrics such as tokens per second and time to first token. Agentic AI breaks that assumption. An agent’s execution is inherently iterative. It repeatedly invokes the model, makes tool calls, incorporates observations, and maintains an increasingly large context throughout the task. As AI agents become an important part of software development, data analysis, and research, these workflows account for a growing share of inference demand. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its KV cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. As models get bigger and inference traffic grows, AI's energy footprint is becoming one of the defining sustainability topics of our time. Every token served draws power, and at scale, that compounds into a significant environmental cost. Currently, the industry’s dominant answer to “how efficient is the infrastructure serving AI inference?” is a single metric: Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE). PUE is a data center level metric that shows how efficiently a building delivers power to its IT equipment. It is useful for a bird’s eye view, but a layer removed from the inference stack itself. A PUE of 1.0 is the theoretical ideal because it would mean that 100% of the energy goes directly to the IT equipment without overhead like cooling. Green contexts address this by letting applications explicitly select a subset of GPU execution resources and target work to those resources directly. Traditional CUDA contexts weren’t designed for this usage model. posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Compaction | Multi-agent systems | Hire the sub-agent | No free lunch | From trees to swarms | What should the swarm look like? Let’s begin with something everyone should be able to agree on: inference scaling works. In fact, it works so well that LLMs are now capable of impressive feats like credibly claiming to have solved a Millennium Prize problem — something that would have seemed absurd before we discovered that inference follows scaling laws. Give a model more compute at test time (let it think longer, call more tools, check its own work) and it will perform better at the task. There’s just one problem: eventually, you run out of context. I mean that literally : you fill the predefined context window. 1 Context windows haven’t been getting much bigger, either: the current frontier models all top out around 1M tokens. You don’t see any serious model with a 100M-token context window, for example. And yet agents these days regularly perform tasks that should be impossible to solve with only 1M tokens of context. How can this be? If you’ve used a coding agent in the last year, you already know the magic trick that explains this discrepancy… compaction! Compaction works like this: as soon as you approach the end of the context window, you ask the agent to write a summary and hand off its work to a fresh context, where that work is picked up until the context window is full again and you have to compact again. You do this until (the agent thinks that) the task is solved. Compaction is amazing. It lets you keep the same agent session going for days (or weeks)…

posts.excerpt: Sections: Optimizations | TileRT | Lightning Indexer | Sparse MLA | MLA Modifications | IndexShare | Pipeline | RL Training Algorithm How does sparse attention affect the TAM of memory, including HBM and NAND? Sparse attention selects top-k most relevant tokens to attend to, reducing the memory consumption and bandwidth requirements during the core Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA) operation. However, the efficiency improvement doesn’t directly translate to overall memory savings in practice . Concretely, the top-k selection operation typically requires the full context to be in HBM, so sparse attention doesn’t eliminate the memory capacity bottleneck. To overcome this limitation, the SGLang team designed HiSparse, a hierarchical memory system that proactively offloads KV cache entries from device HBM to host DRAM. HiSparse behaves like an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache , where it loads tokens from DRAM to HBM upon top-k selection cache miss, and it offloads tokens from HBM to DRAM based on the LRU eviction policy. To reduce the cache miss latency, HiSparse overlaps KV cache loading of layer N with the execution of layer N-1 (layer-wise overlapping), introduced in HiSparse’s prior work HiCache. With HiSparse, SGLang greatly boosts throughput at high concurrency and long context scenarios, at the cost of top-k cache miss I/O overhead. Sparse attention reduces KV cache memory and bandwidth requirements at the SDPA operation, but it does not reduce the overall memory capacity usage. PhD students who cannot wait to graduate, because they want to join a frontier lab and they have concluded that research in academia is meaningless. They are counting the years until they can leave. I believe both stories are wrong, and wrong for the same reason. They assume the future of research belongs to whoever has the most GPUs. I think the opposite is true. Academia is probably about to have a renaissance, and the most exciting work of the next decade will happen in university labs — not in spite of their limited resources, but because of them. posts.title: Accelerating Long-Context and Agentic Inference with NVFP4 KV Cache
posts.summary: The KV cache is a fundamental building block of the modern LLM inference system. The context from multiple conversation rounds in agent sessions is cached as keys and values (KV) in GPU memory, allowing the model to reuse them during subsequent decoding steps.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: NVFP4 KV Implementation in SGLang | NVFP4 KV Decode Attention Kernel Implementation | Experiments and Results | Accuracy | Performance | Decode Performance | Prefill Performance | Agentic Workloads The KV cache is a fundamental building block of the modern LLM inference system. The context from multiple conversation rounds in agent sessions is cached as keys and values (KV) in GPU memory, allowing the model to reuse them during subsequent decoding steps. When generating each new token, the new query token attends to the relevant past KV tokens from the KV cache. As context windows grow, storing and reading KV cache puts increasing pressure on GPU memory capacity and bandwidth. There are two complementary ways to address this pressure: expand the storage available to the cache, or reduce the amount of data stored per token. GPU memory provides fast access to active KV data, but its capacity is limited. A serving system handling many users or long-running sessions cannot keep every session’s cache resident indefinitely. Hierarchical KV Caching (HiCache) extends the cache hierarchy into host memory and distributed storage, allowing the system to retain more context beyond the GPU. KV cache quantization addresses the other side of the problem. Storing K/V values in FP8 instead of BF16 roughly halves the data footprint and reduces the bytes read during decoding. This can improve performance when KV reads are a bandwidth bottleneck. The tradeoff is numerical precision: lower-bit representations introduce quantization error, and that error must remain small enough to…

Nemotron 3.5 Lightning illustrates the answer: It uses a Mixture-of-Experts ( MoE ) architecture that selects only a subset of its parameters for each token . The right choice affects throughput, memory cost, and serving complexity more than raw parameter count does. Therefore, choosing between them comes down to your deployment constraints. Think of the difference like two engines with the same total displacement. One fires every cylinder on every cycle; the other activates only the cylinders it needs. In simple terms, dense and MoE models differ in how they use their parameters. A dense model activates all its parameters for every token. An MoE model stores multiple expert networks but routes each token through only a selected subset. Dense models typically favor simpler, more predictable deployment, while MoE models can deliver greater capacity and throughput when memory and serving complexity are manageable. These workloads combine long contexts and high prefill reuse with sub-agent bursts and numerous tool calls. Long context: system prompts, tool definitions, and the large number of turns make context accumulate quickly. High prefix reuse: since the conversation progresses linearly, where output from turn n-1 is concatenated to turn n (typically), most context can be served from KV cache rather than recomputed (this depends on the amount of storage available to store KV tensors). As n grows, the ratio of cached input relative to uncached typically tends towards 1. Sub-agent bursts: a session launches multiple short-lived sub-agents with fresh context, which create bursty KV-cache patterns. Read more about the methodology in our AgentX article. posts.title: Tiered KV Cache Offloading in vLLM
posts.summary: A host-centric framework for scaling KV cache across host memory, filesystems, object stores, and remote peers — reducing recomputation and increasing serving capacity.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: The Host-Centric Design | Fast accelerator release, just-in-time allocation | Consolidated I/O | Canonical memory layout | Simple secondary tiers | How Offloading and Reloading Work | Offload path | Reload path Long-context models and multi-turn conversations generate massive KV caches. When accelerator memory (e.g., GPU HBM) fills up, previously computed KV data is evicted. On the next request that needs it, vLLM must recompute it from scratch. Tiered KV cache offloading preserves evicted KV data across host memory, storage, and remote peers. Instead of recomputing, vLLM reloads the data from a lower tier — saving compute, reducing latency, and increasing the effective serving capacity of the cluster. With secondary tiers, KV data also becomes shareable across nodes — enabling horizontal scaling of the cache, warm-starting new instances from shared storage, and transferring KV data between peers for disaggregated serving or load balancing. The framework has been available in vLLM since v0.22 and a detailed usage guide can be found here . The core design principle: all KV data flows through host memory (CPU DRAM) . When offloading, KV data moves from accelerator to host first. From the host, it propagates to secondary tiers — filesystem, object storage, or remote peers. When reloading, the flow reverses: a secondary tier promotes data into host memory, then it is loaded to the accelerator. Copying from accelerator to host is a fast local PCIe transfer. Each of those is a shuffle. Shuffle is the one operation Ray Data cannot stream. A map or a write takes a block, transforms it, and passes it downstream, so peak memory tracks block size rather than dataset size. groupby, join, and repartition require every row sharing a key to be gathered in one place, so a shuffle worker holds a partition, and partition size is the dataset divided by the partition count. Ten times the data means ten times the memory in that worker. Shuffle is where these pipelines fail, where the OOMs happen, and where a job that ran fine at 100 GB falls over at 1 TB. Shuffle V2 is a redesign of Ray Data's shuffle engine. posts.summary: Building a real video indexing service on Ray Serve asynchronous inference, and benchmarking it against Amazon SageMaker for scaling, reliability and latency.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: A quick recap: what async inference is for | The application: a video-indexing service | Behavior under load | Comparing against a managed alternative: Amazon SageMaker | End-to-end latency | When async inference is the right fit In an earlier post , we introduced asynchronous inference in Ray Serve: a way to run long-running model calls off the request path, backed by a message queue, with automatic retries and queue-depth autoscaling. This post is a practical follow-up. We build a real service on top of that feature, a video-indexing pipeline, run it under a heavy load, and compare it against a common managed alternative. In serving ML models, some applications make a single model call that runs for several seconds to minutes, e.g. - transcribing an hour of audio, indexing a video, or generating an image or a video. On a normal synchronous HTTP endpoint the request stays open for the whole computation. At millisecond latencies that coupling is invisible, but for calls this long it creates two problems. First, a burst of traffic piles onto a fleet that takes seconds or minutes to finish each request, so the workers fall behind and clients, or any intermediary hop, start timing out. As a result, the service and overall system gets less reliable at exactly the moments you can't predict. posts.summary: Prime Flash MoE is a set of Blackwell-optimized CUDA kernels for the MoE feed-forward pass that keep the intermediate activation on-chip — up to 2.4× faster than PyTorch grouped GEMM, with bf16 and MXFP8 data paths and benchmarks on B200.

Getting data into the tensor cores | For the bf16 weights: one folded rank-4 descriptor | For the tokens: TMA gathers them too Prime Flash MoE is a set of Blackwell-optimized CUDA kernels that avoid materializing certain intermediate tensors and, in the fused configuration avoid materializing the activation as well, thus saving a lot of memory traffic. The kernels are up to 2.4× faster than PyTorch grouped GEMM, and deliver a ~2.3× speedup across the 4k-128k token range. We also integrated the kernel into our prime-rl framework to accelerate the forward pass of MoE models. There are two data paths, one for bf16 and one for MXFP8. They share the same structure and differ in how they feed the tensor cores. Each runs in one of two pipelines, chosen with split : the fused one, where all three operations really are a single kernel launch, and the split one, which is three kernels - a gather, the up projection, and a separate down projection. Why a fused and a split pipeline you may ask? Fusion trades one activation materialization for C partial-output reductions. For our default shape that is roughly 2 KB of activation data versus 32 KB of partial output contributions per routed token-expert pair. At small problem sizes the output accumulator remains cache-resident, making those reductions cheap enough that avoiding the activation round trip wins. posts.title: Unified Radix Cache: One Tree for Hybrid Model Prefix Caching
posts.summary: Prefix caching reuses KV when requests share the same token prefix. Under full attention, once the KV for a shared prefix is computed, it remains valid as more tokens are appended. A later request with the same prefix can reuse those KV entries instead of recomputing them during prefill.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Introduction | Highlights | One Tree, Composable Components | Finding a Safe Reuse Boundary | Component Hooks Across the Tree Lifecycle | Native HiCache Across Memory Tiers | Components, Anchors, and Sidecars | HiCache Multi-Turn Benchmark Results Prefix caching reuses KV when requests share the same token prefix. Under full attention, once the KV for a shared prefix is computed, it remains valid as more tokens are appended. A later request with the same prefix can reuse those KV entries instead of recomputing them during prefill. SGLang tracks this mapping with a radix tree keyed by token sequences. Before prefill, the tree finds the longest reusable prefix and returns its KV locations to the scheduler. Hybrid models break this single reuse rule. A request may combine full attention KV, sliding window attention KV, and recurrent states, each with a different notion of reuse. Full attention KV remains reusable across the entire matched prefix. Sliding window attention KV covers only the trailing window. A recurrent state is valid only at an exact prefix checkpoint. They share the same token prefix, but not the same reusable boundary . Forcing a single boundary across all of them either discards valid reuse or permits invalid reuse. These reuse rules appear in different combinations across model families. Encoding each combination as a specialized cache class creates a combinatorial class matrix, especially once orthogonal capabilities such as HiCache are added. Earlier implementations followed this pattern, duplicating matching, insertion, locking, and eviction…

posts.title: RL Is Bottlenecked by Inference. Scale It Independently.
posts.summary: Agentic RL spends most of every step on inference, not training. Scale inference in RL with SkyPilot Job Groups and slime.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Why agentic RL is inference-bound | The abstraction: disaggregated jobs you scale independently | Scaling the engines instead of the trainer | Run it | What could be improved even further A step of an agentic RL run spends far longer generating rollouts than it spends training on them. So for most of every step, the training GPUs sit idle while generation requests back up on a single inference engine. This isn’t specific to one setup: across recent large-scale RL systems, rollout generation is routinely the single largest wall-clock component of a step ( a growing pile of systems papers all land here). So adding trainer GPUs won’t help, because the trainer already finishes early and then waits. If the bottleneck is inference, that’s the thing to scale, independently of the trainer. This post walks through doing exactly that with slime , an RL post-training framework, on SkyPilot Job Groups . We train a Qwen3-14B coding agent on real bug-fixing tasks and scale the inference fleet from one SGLang engine to three. Async step time falls by almost 50%, from 1200s to 661s, and the trainer config never changes across the whole sweep. A year or two ago, RL post-training mostly meant RLHF on preference pairs. Now a lot of it is verifiable rewards on coding tasks: hand the model a bug, let it produce a fix, and score that fix automatically. Meta’s SWE-RL did this in a single shot, rewarding a patch by its textual similarity to the human fix. The newer work is more agentic: the model acts over many turns, and the reward is a test suite that passes or fails. Last year…

posts.title: Toward a Cleaner Quantization Stack in SGLang
posts.summary: Quantization has moved from an advanced feature to an essential part of high-throughput LLM serving. As the number of checkpoint formats, model architectures, and hardware backends grows, the quantization stack becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: 1. Why This Matters? | 2. A Scheme-Based Quantization Architecture | 3. Benefits: Faster Development and Broader Reuse | 4. Future Work | 5. Acknowledgements | 6. Appendix Quantization has moved from an advanced feature to an essential part of high-throughput LLM serving . As the number of checkpoint formats, model architectures, and hardware backends grows, the quantization stack becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. This post explains the architectural changes proposed in SGLang issue #15194 . The new design separates checkpoint interpretation, parameter registration, weight loading, post-processing, and kernel execution into focused, reusable components. Production serving engines can no longer rely on a single low-bit kernel. They must handle diverse checkpoint formats such as AWQ, GPTQ, Compressed-Tensors, ModelSlim, and Quark; dense and MoE weights; KV cache formats; attention kernels; and hardware-specific execution across CUDA GPUs, Ascend NPUs, CPUs, and other backends. When format parsing, parameter registration, weight loading, post-processing, platform checks, and kernel execution are all placed in one class, each new format or backend increases coupling. The result becomes harder to review, test, reuse, and extend. In the old design, a single quantization method often owned the entire path: defining parameters, loading weights, transforming layouts, selecting a backend, and launching the kernel. Supporting another platform meant adding more branches to the same format-facing class, even when much of the hardware logic could have been reused…

posts.title: A note on the Hugging Face agent incident
posts.summary: Hugging Face published a technical timeline of a recent agent intrusion. Modal's platform and isolation were not compromised in this incident.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Hugging Face published a technical timeline of a recent agent intrusion, which names Modal as the third-party infrastructure the agent used as a launchpad. Modal's platform and isolation were not compromised in any way. The environment involved was a customer's own application. It was deployed to a endpoint that was publicly accessible without authentication, and it was designed to compile and execute code submitted by anyone on the internet in a Modal Sandbox. The code execution the attacker obtained took place inside that customer's own container, within Modal's standard sandbox isolation boundary. No other customer workloads were affected. While customers can expose Sandboxes to unauthenticated traffic, this is never the default, and Modal provides the authentication, network, and monitoring controls to keep production workloads locked down. We recommend that anything exposed to the public internet require authentication , IP allowlist, restrict its outbound network access to only what it needs, and treat any code or input it accepts from users as untrusted. For additional questions, email security@modal.com .

We got there by pushing the cost of a generated image down on every axis we could find, and it helps to see those axes as one equation: the cost of an image is how many forward passes the diffusion transformer runs, times how expensive each pass is. Two fronts. Make each forward pass cheap: run the transformer in FP4, and fuse the small ops around each matmul so they don't pay a memory round-trip. Make the passes fewer: distill classifier-free guidance from two branches into one, and distill the many denoising steps into a handful. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and…

posts.excerpt: Sections: Kaplan et al.’s Scaling Laws | Chinchilla Scaling Laws | Method 1: Fix model sizes, vary the token budget | Method 2: IsoFLOP profiles | Method 3: Parametric fit | Reconciling Kaplan and Chinchilla | Why power law? | Toy simulation Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$. This predictability makes scaling laws highly valuable in practice. A common workflow is to fit scaling laws on a handful of small runs and then extrapolate to estimate the token and compute requirements for larger models. The predictability of generalization error with scale had already been investigated before scaling laws became a mainstream concept. Amari et al. (1992) derived four types of learning curves using a Bayesian approach and the annealed approximation. where $E$ can be 0 and $\alpha = -2, -1, -1/2$. But, if optimized, MSA’s design allows it to cut the per-token attention compute to roughly 1/20th of its full-attention predecessor. MSA splits every attention layer into two parts: which KV to look at, and how to attend to it. The first is solved by introducing an indexing layer. For each query, the indexer scores candidate KV blocks and chooses the top-k blocks. The indexer also maintains a cache of index keys with a single shared head and a small head dimension. By focusing only on top scoring KV cache blocks, MSA only computes the attention of the relevant 128 tokens in the KV caches rather than the full block. The model produces selection in query-major form: for each query, a list of top-k block IDs. The natural kernel follows that shape — loop over queries, gather their selected KV blocks, and then attend. posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: What a typical online RL pipeline looks like | Why GRPO made this worse | Where Slurm’s model breaks down | How every major framework works around it | OpenRLHF | veRL | NeMo RL | TRL Open the Slurm launch script for OpenRLHF . It parses node IPs from scontrol show hostnames , hardcodes service addresses, and bootstraps a Ray cluster by hand. Now open the one for veRL . Same thing. NeMo RL ? Same thing again. Three unrelated frameworks, three sets of nearly identical glue code, all papering over Slurm’s lack of multi-service orchestration. Slurm is a batch scheduler. Online RL - GRPO, PPO, multi-step RLHF - is not a batch job. Writing better launch scripts doesn’t change that. A GRPO or PPO training loop isn’t one program. It’s four or five separate processes that need to coordinate on every iteration. The policy/actor model is where gradient updates happen - you need H100s or B200s with NVLink and InfiniBand here. The rollout engine (usually vLLM or SGLang ) generates completions from the current policy; it’s memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound, so cheaper GPUs work. Then there’s the reward model (or a verifiable reward function) and a reference model for KL divergence penalties - both inference-only, each needing its own GPU allocation. Finally, data processing (tokenization, advantage computation, replay buffers) runs on CPU. These aren’t independent jobs. The rollout engine produces completions, the reward model scores them, advantages get computed, the policy takes a gradient step, and then the updated weights have to ship back to the inference engine…

You may have hundreds of pods, each with thousands of cached blocks. State can change hundreds of times per second. Across this complexity, queries need to return in microseconds because they sit on the critical path of every inference request. A hashmap and a mutex aren’t sufficient for the scale and velocity of inference routing. You need a data structure designed for this specific access pattern: a way to provide fast concurrent reads, batched writes, idempotent event processing, and efficient query responses. posts.title: Systematic Reward Hacking and Prime Sprints
posts.summary: We release tunable RL templates that demonstrate reward hacking at 1B scale and introduce Prime Sprints, an open-access program with sponsored runs for community research.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Motivation | Experiment Design | Key Findings | All backdoor-ifeval Environments | Framework | Results | Rarity Floor | Visible Reward Shape Detecting and mitigating reward hacking is one of the key challenges faced when scaling RL, particularly in semi-verifiable domains. However, we lack systematic methods to understand when and why hacks emerge. Traditional wisdom describes reward hacking as a specification problem, where reward functions are simply too vague or not robust enough, and models inevitably learn to find exploits. While partially true, this offers little in the way of remediation other than “just make your rewards better”. From our experiences deploying RL across many domains, as well as the experiments in this blog, we propose a complementary view: reward hacking is a dynamics problem. We design a suite of backdoor-ifeval environments with IFEval-style tasks and “hidden” keyword rewards, which we use to study hacking systematically. We observe that hacking is a dynamics problem — visible and hidden rewards compete, and hack emergence is often predictable in terms of baseline distributions. We’re releasing the environment behind these findings and launching Sprints - free credits for anyone who wants to run their own reward hacking experiments. More below! There is a core distinction in any RL system between what we want the model to do and what we reward it for doing. The first is a description of intent in human terms. The second is an operational signal that is necessarily simpler than the intent; it has to be measurable. The two are correlated…

posts.summary: SID-1 is an agentic search model that is 24x faster than GPT-5.1-high, 374x cheaper than Sonnet 4.5, and achieves 1.9x higher recall than traditional RAG pipelines. Here's how we trained it using large-scale RL on turbopuffer.

We search, read results, adapt, and search again until we find the information we seek. We're Max and Sam, co-creators of SID-1 , an agentic search model that builds upon this idea. As a result of its training, SID-1 nearly doubles recall over classical retrieval pipelines and outperforms frontier LLMs at orders of magnitude lower latency and cost. SID is a research lab for search. We trained SID-1 using large-scale reinforcement learning (RL), and when training became bottlenecked on search latency, we migrated the search backend to turbopuffer. We wrote this post, on invitation from the turbopuffer team, to share how we train SID models using large-scale, synchronous RL rollouts at 1k+ searches per second over 10M+ document corpora across thousands of training steps. Unlike humans, static retrieval ("RAG") pipelines cannot search iteratively. They run a fixed sequence of steps and return the result, even when it's bad. The conventional fixes are to add more retrieval steps (LLM query rewrites, hybrid search with rank fusion, reranking) or tweak the embedding model or chunking strategy, often at the cost of engineering time, complexity, and brittleness. posts.label: infra

One thing we realized is that the Mojo language is ideally suited to the needs of modern AI coding agents. Mojo has a familiar syntax with minimal boilerplate, so it’s token-efficient for agents to read and write. Its type system and constraint model catch many common errors at compile time. Rather than having an agent chew tons of tokens to build something that may or may not work, then spend hours debugging it when it doesn’t, Mojo catches problems early and provides clear error messages to the agents. This tighter feedback loop is one reason typed languages are increasingly favored for agentic workflows . Mojo also doesn't trade ergonomics for performance. The same code that reads cleanly can target the full range of hardware Mojo supports , including NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple silicon GPUs. The only challenge is that Mojo is still a young language and LLMs haven’t been trained on lots of Mojo code. That’s why we’ve created tools to help agents produce correct, idiomatic Mojo from the start. This starts with open-sourcing of all of the Mojo code we’ve written at Modular , along with all of our Python APIs for MAX. posts.title: Why LLM Inference Needs a New Kind of Router - Part 1
posts.summary: HTTP routing has been a solved problem for many years. Round-robin, consistent hashing, least-connections. Pick one, put it in front of a pool of identical servers, and the traffic spreads pretty evenly.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Years of stateless routing | Where LLMs break the model | KV Cache State | Hardware Specialization | Conversation continuity | Multi-step execution | The three layers | Data Layer HTTP routing has been a solved problem for many years. Round-robin, consistent hashing, least-connections. Pick one, put it in front of a pool of identical servers, and the traffic spreads pretty evenly. The backends here aren't interchangeable web servers. They're GPU pods holding large, local KV caches in high-bandwidth, RAM or SSD memory. That state is expensive to rebuild, not uniformly available across the cluster, and often determines whether a request returns quickly or spends seconds recomputing previous work. Some pods might specialize in prefill, others in decode. Conversations typically stretch across requests. A single inference call sometimes needs two backends in sequence. The old assumptions about "interchangeable backends" and "independent requests" don't support these… Traditional routing is blind to all of this. It treats every backend as interchangeable, every request as independent, every pod as equally good. GPU pods are none of those things. They’re stateful, specialized and heterogeneous. Inference routing has to account for that. This is the first post in a three-part series about what routing has to become to handle inference workloads. Modular Cloud’s orchestration layer is built around this routing problem, and this series explains how it solves it. posts.title: MoE Fundamentals: Why Sparse Models Are the Future of AI
posts.summary: MoE models use under 10% of parameters per token—enabling trillion-parameter scaling without trillion-token compute. Discover how routing changes everything.
posts.label: infra
posts.excerpt: Sections: Why Choose MoE | The Fundamentals of MoE | Citation | The MoE 101 Guide | Router Wars: Which MoE Routing Strategy Actually Works | Debugging Dead MoE Models: A Step-by-Step Guide | MoE at Scale: Making Sparse Models Fast on Real Hardware | MoE Math Demystified: What Does 8x7B Actually Mean? Here's a counterintuitive fact: The most powerful language models today use less than 10% of their parameters for any given token (Yang et al., 2025, DeepSeek-AI et al., 2024). This isn't a bug - it's the feature that makes trillion-parameter models possible. Why does this matter? We've hit a scaling wall. The progression from GPT-3's parameter scaling (Brown et al., 2020) to Chinchilla's compute-optimal ratios (Hoffmann et al., 2022) drove AI training compute up by a factor of 10^21 since AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). But we can't just keep making models bigger forever - as we increase parameters, we need to proportionally increase compute. Eventually it becomes prohibitively expensive to train these models and impossible to sustain. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the path forward. The key mechanism is conditional activation of parameters. While dense transformers activate all parameters for every token (often multiplying many weights by zero activations (Mirzadeh et al., 2023)), MoE models selectively route tokens to a subset of parameters, which allows us to increase total parameter count without a proportional increase in computations per token.
